title: A bowl of red stew (Genesis 25:19–34)
hookLine: twins who wrestle in the womb, and a birthright sold for lentils

lines: TWINS WHO FIGHT IN THE WOMB.
RED AND HAIRY; HOLDING THE HEEL.
cards: Twins, and they fight before they're born. The Torah steps back here, to how Isaac's family began. Rebekah can't have children; Isaac prays for her, and she conceives.
The pregnancy is so hard she asks God why, and the answer is startling. In the old JPS translation: "Two nations are in thy womb." Two peoples, and the elder shall serve the younger.
The first comes out red and hairy all over: Esau. The second comes out holding his brother's heel: Jacob, Yaakov, from akev, heel. Esau grows up a hunter, a man of the fields.
Jacob, the Torah says, is "a quiet man, dwelling in tents." Isaac loves Esau. Rebekah loves Jacob.

teach.b: One day Jacob is cooking stew, and Esau comes in from the field, exhausted: "Let me swallow, I pray thee, some of this red, red pottage; for I am faint." He doesn't even name the food. Just: that red stuff.
That's why, the Torah says, he was called Edom, red. Jacob says: first sell me your birthright.
The birthright, the bechorah, was the firstborn's place: in Deuteronomy, a double share of the inheritance; in Rashi's reading, the family's sacred service too.
Esau shrugs: "Behold, I am at the point to die; and what profit shall the birthright do to me?" He swears, and Jacob hands him bread and lentils.
The verbs come fast as a man eating: he ate, and drank, and rose up, and went his way. Then the Torah's own verdict: "So Esau despised his birthright."
The Talmud says that on that very day, Abraham, their grandfather, had died.

teach.h: LENTILS FOR A HOUSE IN MOURNING.
teach.b: Lentils were a mourner's meal: round, because mourning comes around to everyone.
Jacob was cooking for a house in mourning, and Esau came in from the field without even noticing.
Some readers are uneasy with Jacob too: the Torah blames Esau for selling cheap, but what kind of brother drives that bargain with a starving man? Both can be true.
What's left on the table is the warning: something precious traded for one hot bowl, because it was right there, and you were hungry.

how: Jews read the birth of Jacob and Esau in the Torah portion Toldot; mourners are often served round foods such as lentils or eggs at the first meal after a funeral, a custom linked to this story.

o: the firstborn's rights and place in the family
a sacred vow sworn over a shared family meal

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Esau was born second, holding Jacob's heel
Esau came out first; Jacob came out holding Esau's heel.
the Talmud says Abraham died the day of the stew
and Jacob was cooking lentils, a mourner's meal.

games.q: you're Esau, starving after a day in the field. your brother says: sell me your birthright for this bowl of stew. what do you do?
o: sell it: what good is a birthright if I die?
games.why: he swears it away, eats, drinks, rises and goes. "So Esau despised his birthright."

practice: Think of what you trade too cheaply when you're tired or hungry or bored: sleep for one more episode, a promise to your kid for five more minutes on your phone, your temper for the pleasure of being right, your quiet morning for a scroll.
Pick one and notice the red stew in it, the thing that's right there and hot, and what you give up for it. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Bechorah, Hebrew for the birthright, traded for lentils by a hungry twin.

orig.note: Hebrew: the birthright, the rights of the firstborn.

carryVoice: Your line: don't sell it for stew. Two brothers, one bowl, and a story only just starting. That's day fifty-three.
